content.title: About
content.content: Stew, fish is a dish made from fish slowly simmered in a sauce of vegetables, spices, and sometimes wine. The gentle cooking preserves the delicate flavor of the fish while creating a tender texture and a broth rich in vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fish stew is popular in Mediterranean, Asian, and Scandinavian cuisines.
Traditional preparation uses low heat in clay pots or covered pans.
Different fish species (cod, salmon, pike) give distinct flavor notes.
Adding tomatoes, lemon juice, or wine enhances aroma and antioxidant content.
Fish stew is often served with whole grains, potatoes, or fresh herbs.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Fish provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Stewed fish, especially from fatty varieties, supplies EPA and DHA, supporting heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish retains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Fish is abundant in iodine, selenium, and phosphorus, which aid thyroid function and bone health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with modest oil, the stew remains heart‑friendly.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions, ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Contaminant risk
items.content: Certain fish can contain mercury or other toxins; choose small‑to‑medium species from reputable sources.

items.title: Overcooking
items.content: Excessive simmering can make the fish dry and harder to digest.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Broths often contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stew hot with its sauce alongside a side such as mashed potatoes, rice, couscous, or fresh vegetables. Garnish with herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or capers for brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers in an airtight container and refrigerate for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze up to 3 months after fully cooling and portioning.

tea-iced-bottled-black-decaffeinated-die.title: Iced Bottled Black Decaffeinated Diet Tea

content.title: About
content.content: Iced black decaffeinated diet tea in a bottle is a ready‑to‑drink beverage made from selected black tea leaves that have undergone a decaffeination process. The drink is sweetened with artificial sweeteners, making it low‑calorie, and sealed in a hermetic glass or plastic bottle.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually performed by water‑extraction or CO₂ methods, preserving the tea’s flavor profile.
Black tea retains polyphenols even after the caffeine is removed.
Iced tea is a popular summer refreshment because it quickly quenches thirst.
Diet versions use sucralose or stevia instead of sugar, reducing calories to 0–5 kcal per 100 ml.
Bottle packaging protects the drink from light and oxygen, extending shelf life.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Polyphenols in black tea help neutralize free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Regular consumption of black tea has been linked to modest reductions in blood pressure.

items.title: Improved digestion
items.content: Tannins stimulate gastric juice secretion, aiding the digestion of meals.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: The diet version contains virtually no calories, making it suitable for weight‑control diets.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Iced tea provides fluid intake, especially useful in hot weather.

items.title: Tea allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to tea components.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some people are sensitive to sucralose or other sweeteners, which can cause gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Tannins may affect the absorption of certain drugs, such as iron supplements.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: A modest amount of salt is sometimes added for flavor; those with hypertension should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chill the bottle, open, and drink straight. The tea can also serve as a base for cocktails, or be garnished with a slice of lemon or fresh mint for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bottle in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Plain tortilla chips are crisp, thin slices made from corn tortillas that are fried or baked until golden. They contain no added flavors, making them a versatile base for dips, guacamole, salsa, or as a snack on their own.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tortilla chips originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a way to use leftover corn tortillas.
Traditionally they are made from whole‑grain corn flour, which makes them gluten‑free.
In Mexico similar chips are called “totopos” and are often served with lime and salt.
Tortilla chips are a key component of dishes like nachos and taco salads.
Legend says the first chips were created by accident when a tortilla was over‑fried until crisp.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Corn flour provides slow‑releasing energy, helping to keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for people with gluten intolerance when made from pure corn flour.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports healthy digestion and gut microbiota.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Plain chips contain no added sugars, making them a better choice for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Corn provides carotenoids and phenolic compounds that have antioxidant properties.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Some brands are heavily salted, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Crispy chips are calorie‑rich, so they should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to corn products.

items.title: Trans fats in some brands
items.content: If fried in partially hydrogenated oils, chips may contain trans fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Plain tortilla chips are served with dips (salsa, guacamole, cheese sauce), used in nachos, added to salads for crunch, or enjoyed straight from the bag. They can be reheated briefly in the oven to restore crispness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chips in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer them to a tightly sealed bag to maintain crunch and prevent moisture absorption.

content.title: About
content.content: Yogurt NFS is a fermented dairy product made by inoculating whole milk with specific bacterial cultures. It has a smooth, creamy taste with a mild tang and a velvety texture. The product is offered in various fat levels and flavor additions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Yogurt is one of the oldest fermented milk foods, traced back to ancient Egypt.
The bacteria Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus used in yogurt aid digestion.
NFS yogurt is often fortified with probiotics, vitamin D and B12 to boost its nutritional profile.
In many cultures yogurt is traditionally served with honey, nuts or fresh berries.
Fermentation reduces lactose, making yogurt more tolerable for people with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Live cultures support gut microbiota balance and strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Calcium in yogurt is essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Provides protein
items.content: Yogurt supplies high‑quality dairy protein that helps tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt contains riboflavin (B2) and cobalamin (B12), important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low‑fat options
items.content: Light versions are suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to yogurt.

items.title: Added sugar in flavored varieties
items.content: Sweetened yogurts increase calorie intake and can contribute to tooth decay.

items.title: Live culture viability
items.content: Probiotic counts may decline if stored at high temperatures for long periods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Yogurt NFS can be enjoyed on its own, blended into smoothies, mixed with oatmeal or granola, or used in sauces and desserts. For extra creaminess it is often combined with honey, berries or nuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep yogurt refrigerated at 1 °C–4 °C. After opening, consume within 3–5 days. Do not freeze, as the texture may change.
